result: The study used serial block face scanning electron microscopy (SBEM) to obtain 3D reconstructions of over 7000 spines and their parallel fiber synapses in the mouse cerebellar posterior vermis (lobule VI). Three experimental groups were analyzed: spontaneous wake (W, n=4), extended wake/sleep deprivation (EW, n=4), and sleep (S, n=6), with mice spending ~86%, 100%, and ~84% of the last 6-8 hours in their respective states. A total of 96 dendritic branches were segmented across all mice, yielding 7388 spines, of which 6853 had synapses and 6618 had fully measurable axon-spine interfaces (ASIs).
evaluation: The methodological claims are well-documented with specific quantitative details about sample sizes, imaging parameters, and data collection. The use of the same mice as in previous cortical and hippocampal studies (C50, C51) strengthens the comparative value. The experimental design appropriately controls for circadian effects and sleep deprivation by including three groups (C55). Statistical details and imaging specifications are provided in methods and tables.

result: The absolute density of spines and synapses did not change significantly across experimental groups (spines: p=0.1774; synapses: p=0.1476). Dendritic branches were very spiny with an average density of ~2 spines per μm² of dendrite surface area, and 92.7% of spines contained a synapse, with almost all spines containing only one synapse.
evaluation: These findings are supported by appropriate statistical analysis using linear mixed effects (LME) models with condition as fixed effect and mouse as random intercept (C69, C70). The quantitative data are consistent across groups and align with previous anatomical studies (C68). Sample sizes are adequate (96 dendrites, 7388 spines) for detecting differences if present.

result: The density and proportion of spines without synapses ('naked' spines) showed significant sleep/wake differences. Naked spines were 58% higher in density after sleep compared to spontaneous wake (p=3e-5), representing ~10% of all spines after sleep versus ~5% after wake (p=0.0014). Conversely, spines with synapses represented ~95% of all spines in wake conditions but only ~90% after sleep.
evaluation: The statistical evidence is robust with highly significant p-values from LME models and post-hoc tests (C71, C72, C74). The bidirectional changes in naked versus synapse-bearing spines are internally consistent and quantitatively well-characterized. The effect sizes are substantial (58% increase, doubling of proportion) and statistically significant across multiple comparisons.

result: Branched synapses (two or more synapses on spines sharing the same neck) showed dramatic sleep/wake differences. The absolute density of branched synapses was twofold higher after wake compared to sleep (p=0.0013), with post-hoc tests confirming significant differences (S<EW, p=2e-5; S<W, p=0.0141). Branched synapses represented ~16-17% of all spines after wake but only ~8% after sleep. In 93% of cases, branched synapses contacted boutons from different parallel fibers.
evaluation: This is a major finding with strong statistical support from LME models and post-hoc tests (C85, C86, C87). The twofold difference is substantial and highly significant. The structural characterization showing that 93% of branched synapses contact different parallel fibers (C94) is important for mechanistic interpretation. The consistency across both wake conditions (W and EW) strengthens the finding.

result: The decrease in branched synapses after sleep can account for the overall increase in the proportion of naked spines. The data suggest that during sleep, branched spines lose one or both synapses, or are converted to single spines, while opposite changes occur during wake.
evaluation: This integrative interpretation (C102, C126) is well-supported by the quantitative data showing that the magnitude of branched synapse decrease (~0.2 synapses per dendrite surface area) corresponds well with the increase in naked spines (~0.1 per dendrite surface area), accounting for variability. The mechanistic interpretation (C103, C104) is appropriately presented as a suggestion based on the cross-sectional data, though longitudinal imaging would be needed for definitive proof.

result: Parallel fiber synapses showed homogeneous morphology (club-shaped, synapses on spine side) and a unimodal distribution of ASI sizes with mainly small/medium synapses. No significant effect of sleep/wake condition was found on mean ASI (p=0.0664) or cumulative ASI (p=0.9098). However, branched synapses had significantly smaller average ASI than non-branched synapses (p=0.0002). Most spines contained smooth endoplasmic reticulum, and other ultrastructural features did not change across groups except for spinula proportion.
evaluation: The lack of ASI size changes is well-supported by appropriate LME models controlling for dendrite diameter (C113, C114). The finding that branched synapses are smaller (C115) is statistically significant and mechanistically interesting. The morphological characterizations (C105-C108) are consistent with cited literature. The unimodal distribution (C112) contrasts with cortex/hippocampus and is important for understanding regional differences.

result: Sleep/wake effects on cerebellar parallel fiber synapses differ mechanistically from cortex and hippocampus. In cerebellum, sleep and wake affect the number of branched synapses and proportion of spines with synapses, but not average synaptic strength (ASI size). In contrast, cortex and hippocampus show changes in ASI size but not synapse number. Despite different mechanisms, all three regions show more/stronger synapses after wake than sleep. The unimodal distribution of cerebellar ASI sizes (versus log-normal/bimodal in cortex/hippocampus) suggests plastic changes occur via all-or-none mechanisms rather than graded size changes.
evaluation: This comparative analysis is well-supported because the same 14 mice were used across studies (C135), eliminating inter-animal variability. The mechanistic differences are clearly documented with appropriate statistics. The inference about all-or-none plasticity (C139) is reasonable given the narrow ASI size distribution. The regional differences are notable and biologically plausible given different synaptic properties.

result: The authors propose that branched synapses may represent 'eloquent' (functionally effective) synapses while non-branched synapses may be silent or weak. This interpretation is supported by convergent evidence: (1) electrophysiological studies show 70-80% of parallel fiber synapses are silent or too weak to produce somatic responses, (2) only 7% of stimulated granule cells generate somatic responses versus 54% expected anatomically, (3) the proportion of eloquent synapses from functional studies (~10-20%) matches the proportion of branched synapses observed morphologically (~17% after wake, ~8% after sleep), and (4) modeling studies suggest coincident inputs are needed to drive Purkinje cell firing.
evaluation: While the correlation between functional (~10-20% eloquent) and structural (~8-17% branched) proportions is intriguing (C147), this remains speculative (C140). The supporting evidence from electrophysiology and modeling (C141-C150) is from cited literature, not from the current study. The hypothesis is plausible and well-reasoned, but direct functional testing of branched versus non-branched synapses would be needed to confirm this interpretation. The authors appropriately present this as a possibility rather than a proven mechanism.

result: The authors propose that branched synapses may represent structural correlates of learning through coincidence detection during wake. Supporting this interpretation: (1) 93% of branched synapses contact different parallel fibers, (2) ~50% of parallel fibers traversing Purkinje cells don't synapse with them, providing potential for new contacts, (3) coincident firing mediates associative plasticity, (4) in hippocampal dentate gyrus, branched synapses increase after stimulation and LTP, and (5) given the large number of parallel fiber synapses and spontaneous granule cell activity, spurious coincidences are inevitable. Sleep may promote off-line pruning of branched synapses formed due to spurious coincidences.
evaluation: This mechanistic interpretation is speculative but well-reasoned. The structural observation that branched synapses contact different fibers (C152) is data-supported and important. The analogy to hippocampal plasticity (C157) provides some support, though different brain regions may operate differently. The logic about spurious coincidences (C158) is sound given the anatomy. However, this remains a hypothesis requiring functional validation through experiments tracking learning-induced changes or testing the functional consequences of branched synapse formation/elimination. The authors appropriately present this as a suggested interpretation.

result: The authors propose mechanistic explanations for why cerebellar synaptic renormalization during sleep occurs via branched synapse elimination rather than AMPA receptor removal (as in cortex/hippocampus). Parallel fiber synapses are small and homogeneous in size, leaving little room for strength reduction via receptor removal. Small spines with fewer receptors may be more susceptible to disappearance due to weaker cytoskeletal anchoring. Branched synapses may be especially vulnerable because their average ASI is smaller than non-branched synapses. If branched synapses are eloquent, their pruning would naturally erase traces of spurious coincidences. The removal may trigger PSD disappearance, presynapse detachment, and eventual spine elimination.
evaluation: This mechanistic model is speculative but logically constructed from the data. The observation that branched synapses have smaller ASI (C168) is data-supported (p=0.0002). The inference about limited room for receptor-based plasticity (C166) is reasonable given the unimodal size distribution. However, the proposed sequence of events (C169) and the vulnerability hypothesis (C167) require direct experimental testing. The authors acknowledge this is speculative and suggest two-photon imaging experiments to test it (C170). The model is plausible but remains unproven.

result: Cerebellar glutamatergic synapses follow different plasticity rules than forebrain synapses. Long-term potentiation of parallel fiber synapses relies on GluR3-containing AMPA receptors (not GluR1 as in cortex/hippocampus) and involves increased channel open probability rather than receptor trafficking, thus not expected to increase synapse or ASI size. Long-term depression involves GluR2-containing AMPA receptor endocytosis. The glutamate receptor delta 2, specifically expressed in parallel fiber synapses and involved in LTD and synapse maintenance, shows upregulated mRNA after sleep in transcriptomic analysis.
evaluation: These claims about cerebellar plasticity mechanisms are well-supported by cited literature (C172, C173, C175, C176). The transcriptomic finding about delta 2 upregulation after sleep (C177) is from the authors' previous work. This provides important context for understanding why ASI size doesn't change with sleep/wake in cerebellum—some forms of cerebellar LTP don't involve receptor insertion or size changes (C174). The authors appropriately note that whether delta 2 changes contribute to the observed synaptic changes is unknown and requires future study (C178).

result: The study has important limitations regarding generalizability. Due to labor-intensive methods, only a restricted portion of cerebellar cortex (vermal lobule VI) containing zebrin II-positive Purkinje cells was examined. Zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative Purkinje cells differ in many structural and functional parameters including climbing fiber input, excitability, and plasticity (with zebrin-negative cells showing stronger plasticity). The extent to which results extend to zebrin-negative cells is unknown.
evaluation: The authors appropriately acknowledge these limitations (C180, C183). The restriction to zebrin II-positive cells (C181) is well-documented, and the functional differences between cell types (C182, C184) are supported by cited literature. This is an important caveat that appropriately qualifies the generalizability of the findings. The acknowledgment of this limitation is scientifically appropriate and does not undermine the validity of the findings within the studied population.

result: The introduction establishes the background context: multiple evidence shows excitatory synaptic strength is greater after wake than sleep in rodent cortex and hippocampus, with sleep-associated synaptic weakening serving functions in energy control, memory consolidation, and preventing saturation. The cerebellum is highly plastic with Purkinje cells receiving ~175,000 parallel fiber inputs, which undergo various forms of plasticity linked to learning. However, whether sleep and wake affect cerebellar parallel fiber synapses was completely unknown prior to this study.
evaluation: These background claims are well-supported by extensive citations to prior literature (C1, C21-C45). The claims about cerebellar anatomy and plasticity (C37-C44) are established facts. The identification of the knowledge gap (C8, C45) appropriately motivates the study. This provides essential context for interpreting the novel findings.

result: The discussion contextualizes findings within existing knowledge: sleep and wake profoundly affect cortical and hippocampal synaptic activity and plasticity. The cerebellum contains the largest number of neurons and synapses in the brain, mostly between parallel fibers and Purkinje cells. Very little was known about sleep/wake effects on cerebellar physiology, though Purkinje cell activity is lower during NREM sleep. The current study shows the cerebellum also exhibits ultrastructural synaptic changes consistent with upregulation during wake and down-selection during sleep, though via different mechanisms than forebrain.
evaluation: These contextual and summary claims accurately represent the literature (C118, C195-C199) and appropriately frame the study's contribution (C200, C201). The summary of findings (C201) is consistent with the data presented. This provides appropriate scientific context for the novel findings.

result: The discussion notes that in cerebral cortex, sleep/wake changes in synapses are accompanied by changes in astrocytic processes (glycogen granules, proximity to synaptic cleft, phagocytosis). Bergmann glia in cerebellum establish extensive contacts with parallel fiber synapses, respond to parallel fiber stimulation with calcium increases, modulate Purkinje cell activity, express AMPA receptors required for synapse development, and are involved in phagocytosis that increases after motor learning. Future experiments should test whether sleep and wake affect Bergmann glia structure and function.
evaluation: These claims about astrocytic/glial involvement are well-supported by cited literature (C185-C193). The suggestion for future research (C194) is appropriate given the known roles of Bergmann glia. This identifies an important direction for future investigation that could provide mechanistic insights into the observed synaptic changes.

result: The authors conclude that selective changes in branched synapses suggest that during wake, coincident firing over parallel fibers may translate into formation of synapses on the same branched spine (especially effective at driving Purkinje cells), while during sleep, off-line activity may lead to pruning of branched synapses formed due to spurious coincidences. This interpretation is consistent with evidence that many parallel fiber synapses are silent and that information storage is promoted when only some synapses are effective.
evaluation: This concluding interpretation (C202, C203) synthesizes the findings into a coherent model but remains speculative. The consistency with prior literature (C204, C205) provides some support, but the mechanistic claims about coincidence detection and spurious pruning require direct functional validation. The authors appropriately acknowledge this is speculative. The model is plausible and testable but not yet proven by the current data.
